applications.content: © 2019 JETIR June 2019, Volume 6, Issue 6 www.jetir.org (ISSN-2349-5162) JETIR1906P84 Journal of Emerging Technologies and Innovative Research (JETIR) www.jetir.org 583 STUDY OF TRIBAL ART: HASE CHITTARA FROM KARNATAKA Ms Hemalatha S Ganiger, Dr. Vibha Lodhi Abstract: This article is to introduce Hase chittara, the unique wall painting from Karnataka, a long-established custom practiced by tribal women of Deevaru community in Malnad region of Karnataka. Deevaru or Arya Idiga belongs to Hindu community and they are mainly located in Karnataka. In ancient days, this Deeevaru community involved in developing the Soma and Ayurvedic medicines hence belong to Somvanshi Kshatriy or Chandravanshi Kshatriyas. In ancient Kannada the word Deevaru might have been derived from the Sanskrit word Dweep which means island. Unique wall painting Hase chittara is traditionally practiced b y tribal women of Deevaru community. This exquisite painting is owned by ladies of Deevaru community only. This art is based on themes & originally done on special occasions such as festivals, weddings & auspicious days on the walls of houses , bamboo baskets and earthen pots. Hase chitra signifies the unity of the community where the members of Deevaru community get together to beautify or decorate their houses for the occasions. The aim of this paper is to study old age traditional tribal painting Hase chittara from Karnataka. This study employs content analysis and is based on secondary sources such a s books, journal articles, tribal literature and monographs. The main objectives of this study are to describe the ritualistic relevance of this tribal art form and to locate the current status of this art form in the context of tribal development. The imp act of changing society is visible in the themes of Hase chittara paintings. However need of the hour is to preserve their art and use it for the development of the Deevaru tribe of Karnataka. IndexTerms – Tribe, Deevaru Community, Traditions, Hase chittara, Motifs I. INTRODUCTION According to Oxford Dictionary “tribe is a group of people in primitive or barbarous stage of development, acknowledging the authority of a chief and usually regarding them as having a common ancestor”. As Verrier Elwin (1963) explains, the term and the concept ‘tribe’ is derived from a Latin root, the middle English term “tribuz” meaning the three divisions into which the early Romans were grouped, came to evolve into the modern English ‘tribe’. According to I.L.O. Convention 107 (1957) the aboriginals or tribal have been defined as the tribal or semi-tribal groups of the independent countries deprived socially or economically and having their own customs, traditions and traits or also they have their own special customary laws/conventions”. The constitution of India identifies the indigenous peoples as “tribes”. According to the 2001 Census, India has a tribal population of 8.2% of its total population. Social structure of Tribes maybe identified in two- ways: I. formation of the society on the basis of the kinship which empowered them to be a multifunctional grouping; II. In India, tribes are defined in reference to the cultural practices of certain groups in relation to the mainstream Hindu cultural practices. Folk arts and Tribal arts overlap. Folk arts and crafts are like the head and tail of a coin. They are interrelated in their day today life in terms of tools or objects which are generally used at home, in festivals, customs and rituals. Folk and tribal art, passed from one generation to the next, is the creative expression of people who live in harmony with nature. Traditionally, these art forms, though sometimes purely decorative, were used to mark different occasions such as celebration s, events to pacify malevolent deities or forces of nature, thanksgiving, harvests, and the birth of a child, puberty, marriage and cultural festivals. Indian Folk and Tribal Paintings by Charu. Smita. Gupta The rural folk arts and crafts of India bear distinctive colorful designs which are interwoven with religious and mystical motifs. Each state in India is well-known for multiple folk art forms. As we have seen that Art and craft in Tribal communities is very vital part of their life. It’s not just for sake of doing it, they do as it actually reflects their culture which is very closely related to other components like music, dance, drama etc. They are all interrelated as while doing paintings they also sing which is related to the same theme, each one does not have separate identity. In fact all these are vital part of tribal life. They have a close rapport with one another. They don’t co-exist; in fact it is fundament form of one art in indigene life. Whatever may be the occasion, dancing and singing, which is immediately reflected in the painting which they draw on the walls. As food and water are very important to life, similarly art, dance and music are almost as important as food in the tribe’s life, it would not be an exaggeration to say that. Every night, regularly, these folks dance and sing songs. Perhaps it is a means to break the monotony and fatigue of the day's work and also an easy and handy entertainment. On any special occasion, their enthusiasm is incomparable. They are so engrossed in dancing and singing that they forget their ill feelings and enjoy themselves till the dawn breaks. These occasions also inspire them to compose songs spontaneously though there might not be profound and deep intellectual meaning. There are some festival songs which have been sung for generations. In tribal communities all art forms are equally important and without each other they a re incomplete or impede. They have the necessary musical instruments too. Karnataka is always recognized for its performing folk arts such as Thogalu Gombeyaata, Dollu Kunitha, Karadimajalu, Lavani, Bhootharadhane, Karaga, Bayalaata, Kamsaale, etc. However, not many are aware of the existence of a painting tribal art form named Chittaara or Chittara. Chittara is an art form that includes a set of auspicious geometric motifs and figures celebrating life, practiced in a tribal community called Deewaru which for long been an agrarian community worshiping nature. This Tribal community is native to Shivmogha district of Karnataka living in the enchanted tropic forest of western ghats and found in around the taluk of Sagara predominantly in the villages like Hasunvanthe, Honnemaradu and Majina Kaanu etc. Deewaru community “mainly cultivate rice, sugar cane and areca nut. They are mostly t enants of farm lands; illiterate and financially backward”. Asis De (Chacko & Basant, 2017) It is a matriarchal society where women are highly respected and controls most of the activities. This power relationship between men and women is also manifested in social practices like wedding ceremonies where the bride’s family commands higher respect. Every community is integrated culturally by unique ritualistic practices and customs. These practices reflect their interacti on and © 2019 JETIR June 2019, Volume 6, Issue 6 www.jetir.org (ISSN-2349-5162) JETIR1906P84 Journal of Emerging Technologies and Innovative Research (JETIR) www.jetir.org 584 profound relationship with the environment. The traditions and ritualistic practices of the community are incomplete without the art practice of Chittara. Hase ch ittara is a tribal art practice d by women of Deevaru community which is a matriarchal and agrarian commuinty and whoships nature as nature is very vital part of their cultural. This community basically resides in and aroud Sagar, Karnataka. Earlier main profession of this community was toddy tapping, brewing arrack etc, but due to modernization many people have moved out and very few are now in this traditional job. This exquisite art of Hase chittara is owned by Deevaru community only. Hase chittara of Karnataka is a traditional drawing done by the Deevaru community women on various rituals and occasions on the walls and floor of mud houses. This art is based on themes done on special occasions such as festivals, weddings & auspicious days on the walls of houses. This art symbolizes the unity of the community who help each other and come together to decorate. Hase Chittara draw ings are convoluted designs which signifies the auspicious ceremony and customary way of their life, indicates in geometric patterns. Drawing of hase chittara requires great understanging of proortions and ratios which the women of Deevaru commuinity have been using with great adroitness. The paintings are usually 2-3 feet in size, aesthetically refined, made of symbols representing their physical environment. Eco friendly natural colours like, for white colour rice powder is used, black – roasted rice powder, red colour- red mud and yellow – locally grown berry i.e. Gurige kai is used and brush is made from Pundi naar which is kind of Jute. Chittara paintings are a source of great joy, beauty and creativity for women of Deevaru community. II. PROBLEM DEFINITION Most of our Tribal art traditions are at its urge of becoming extinct. But still, there are resources to help them out. The analysis from primary data collected as well as the information obtained from credible authentic secondary reports, have led to infer that globalization has triggered the emergence of a synthetic macro-culture. This synthetic macro-culture is gaining popularity day by day and silently engineering the gradual attenuation of tribal/ folk art and culture. The twenty first century, the age of globalization, is marked by the incidence of cultural crisis. It is the era where the originality of many tribal and folk cultural and art forms are either losing, being completely forgotten or unknown. Due to globalization, there has been negative influence in the cultural, social, and economic arenas. Exclusivity of our indigenous culture is getting desolate and traditional culture gradually changing by a westernized culture which is fostered and fomented by rampant consumerism and leaving a big impact on the 3rd world countries and deteriorating cultural identity. Due to increase in globalization, it has exerted its voracious effect on culture, society, socio economy, policy, as well as religion The contemporary global trend exhibits that global ization is discouraging indigenous tribal art and culture and strongly catalyzing the promotion of the western culture. The deterioration in the development and growth of tribal culture has resulted into devastating of different aspects like fragmentation of social-cohesion, dilution of cultural identity, and leaving a negative impact on rural economy. Globalization has engineered the massive change in the traditional and cultural arena, different parts of the world are slowly coming under the clutches of an all-pervasive boundless macro culture. As a result the exclusive micro cultures that retain our cultural identity are on the verge of extinction. Because of synthetic macro culture influenced by west, Indigenous cultural forms are becoming endangered which is toppling the socio-cultural structure of the regions having weaker economy. The available literature on tribal art leaves one far from adequate. There is great need and scope to know tribal art and art forms. Unfortunately in depth studies of tribal life, culture of tribal art are indeed rare. This study of tribal art is an attempt to bridge this gap. III. OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY 1. To study the traditional tribal art of Karnataka ; Hase chittara art 2. To explore and document the colors, motifs, materials and process used in art 3. To study the impact of traditional tribal art of Karnataka in contemporary fashion. IV.RESEARCH METHODOLOGY Traditional tribal art of Karnataka; Hase chittara art form is taken and is being studied and researched. This study is based on experiment and survey. Research will be based on the basis of history, development of the art and its contemporary status. Research work will be a humble attempt to bring out this ancient rich treasure to the field o f the discipline of visual art. Study region is a dominated tribal district. Data’s can be categorized into forms two. 1. Primary Data - Data collected from people through direct conversation, using in-depth interviews as a tool for data collection. 2. Secondary Data -The secondary data will be collected by analysing history designs, literature on history, research articles, publications, libraries, newspaper articles, paper clips, internets, journals, websites and others related to the research will be collected, analysed and documented. IV. LITERATURE REVIEW India has rich folk and tribal tradition. Modern man has drawn the political and cultural boundaries but the tribal people ha ve been in forests and in hilly area which has molded their lives. Tribal art is folk art but folk art also can be non -tribal, both are connected deeply to the community. The knowledge of art and craft in tribal community has been transmitted orally from generation to generation. The art emerges from day today life of the community and mold by the environment in which they live. Art, craft, Songs and dances of different tribal communities vary from each other because of the terrain in which they live and also the lifestyle, rituals and customs also vary from one tribe to another but for most of the tribal communities, they worship nature and it plays vital role in their life. The word folk means a group of people living within the given area who have common cultural heritage and some common traits like religion, language, occupation etc. Tribal art is influenced by nature and the tools used in day today life and there is no individual artist in the tribe or folk art, it is a group or community. Any painting the group of people are invo lved in creating that art and the motifs are basically related to religious and nature plays vital role in it. It is an integral part of living. There is no distinction between art and life in tribal societies. © 2019 JETIR June 2019, Volume 6, Issue 6 www.jetir.org (ISSN-2349-5162) JETIR1906P84 Journal of Emerging Technologies and Innovative Research (JETIR) www.jetir.org 585 In most of the tribal communities it is inherited culture to transmit knowledge orally. In the formation of an identity of society, religion has a very important role. Every tribal community has a social structure with unique customs, systems of beliefs and practices. In establishing and reforming of tribal customs and practices, arts, crafts and beliefs play a very important role. Deevara Makkalu, Dhatri Pustaka 2009 by Dr.H S Mohanchandra Gutti Ethnicity is another vital element which contributes to the identity creation. Every folk or tribal art and cultur e forms have an ethnic nature. The art forms are influenced by the myths of a particular region. The ethnic natures of these folk-art forms are maintain their ethnic through which they make socialization possible and they regulate and harmonize them with other communities. In the formation of social structure of these communities, religion and ethnic culture play a vital role and these societies consist of structural units based on structural pluralism. Folk songs, arts and crafts play an important role in their survival. Th ey stand in relation to the power system in every society. Economic status, caste and gender are related to power system. Folklore opposes the power structure and compromise with it and help preserve ethnic identity also. In social identity, gender has an important role. Idealistically in the world of Indian rights and rituals there is no gender inequality and it is evident at the practical lev el. All this can be analyzed in relation to the worship of mother -goddess. In Indian society a social system based on male domination is prevalent. But we see in folk-arts a system that worships woman and attributes mystic qualities to her. It appears mainly in the form of the worship of goddess ‘Kali’ (the dominant icon of Mother Goddess that is worshipped all over India) and at the same time, in all societies gender domination was and is prevalent to the present day 4.1 DEEVARU COMMUNITY The Deevaru community is agricultural, so the cycle of sowing and harvesting has remained the backbone of legendry narratives, which express each and every emotion of a farming community. The astonishingly beautiful Hase chittara; are entwined with nature- as the life of the creators of these paintings are entwined together with nature. Surprisingly, this is the unique aspect of these tribal artisans which they themselves do not realize, that; the whole world of art lovers is fascinated towards! An artist has to develop her (his) own identity in terms of style, technique, choice of colors, etc. For this purpose one has to study the available art traditions. Hase chittara is very rich in forms, styles, creativity and presentation of life and nature. Research work will be a humble attempt to bring out this ancient rich treasure to the field of the discipline of visual art for the first time. Study region is a dominated tribal district. Any unique cultural factor of the tribes has to be utilized for their own economic or social benefit. An in -depth empirical study of the Hase chittara art may bring about newer insights regarding the ways to use their art form for their own development and progress along with preservation of their art form. Unique wall painting Hase chittara is traditionally practiced by tribal women of Deevaru community in Malnad region of Karnataka. Arya Idiga belongs to Hindu community and they are mainly located in Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and other parts of India. Deevaru or Arya Idiga belongs to Hindu community and they are mainly located in Karnataka. In ancient days, this Deeevaru community involved in developing t he Soma and Ayurvedic medicines hence belong to Somvanshi Kshatriy or Chandravanshi Kshatriyas. In ancient Kannada the word Deevaru might have been derived from the Sanskrit word Dweep which means island. It is also said that the word Ida or Eda means Toddy which is derived from archaic Kannada word. Idigas are also known by various names like Namadhari, Halepaika, Billava, Thiyya, Namadhari naik in coastal part of Karnataka. Malenadina Halepaikaru (2016) by N Hucchappa Mastara Kugve and N.Shivananda Kugve Deevaru which means islanders in some parts of Karnataka. And also known as deevaru which means islanders in some parts of Karnataka. Another theory is that the word Eda or Ida is derived from archaic kannada word Ira for Toddy. Earlier main profession of this community was toddy tapping, brewing arrack etc., but due to modernization many people have moved out and very few are now in this traditional job. This exquisite art of Hase chittara is owned by Deevaru community only. Hase chittara of Karnataka is a traditional drawing done by the Deevaru community women on various rituals and occasions on the walls and floor of mud houses. This art is based on themes done on special occasions such as festivals, weddings & auspicious days on the walls of houses. This art symbolizes the unity of the community who help each other and come together to decorate. Hase chittara of Karnataka have not been much explored; hence, efforts have been made in this study to take inspiration from this traditional folk art to incorporate them in the ever expanding field of textile designing. Efforts are being made in the study to provide a strong platform to Hase chittara, whic h is at the verge of extinction due to modernization. Chittara is an autochthonous art practice by Deevaru community –residing in and around Shimoga District, Karnataka. 4.2HASE CHITTARA Hase chittara are created by using very basic shapes: circles, triangles and squares. The art is inspired by observing the nature, circle represents the moon and sun, and triangle represents the pointed trees and mountains. The base for this art is mud paint made from different soils ranging from red, brown, white and yellow. The white color signifies purity and very auspicious and scared. The colors are basically rice flour (akki hittu), red mud (Kemmannu) coal (masi kenda), locally grown berries (kaare kai and gurage kai), lime stone (sunna), turmeric, milk, etc. which are used in making natural colors like white, black, red and yellow. The patterns are basically geometric, the combinations of lines, circles, rectangles, etc. “The interesting thing about it is that our folk artists used mud and herbal colors with rice, leaves or seeds. They didn't use a brush, they used paddy sticks. All the materials were 100 per cent loca l. They used only red and white. But I experiment with different colors. Our area in Malnad has so many different colors of soils.” Radhakrishna. Bandagadde, The Hindu, Crafts from the heart, Bangalore November 22 2011 These tribal art depicts the life style of community like dance, marriage, haunting farming etc. Each painting is usually an entire scene that contains various elements of nature including people, animals, trees, hills etc. Malnad region of Sagara and Shimoga – Hasuvanthe, Honemaradu and Manjina Kaanu. It is a matriarchal society. The traditions and ritualistic practices of the community are incomplete without the art practice of Chittara. Hase chittara are generally 2 – 3 feet in size. Themes based on special occasions such as festivals, weddings & auspicious days. The designs of Hase Chittara like Hasse Gode Chittara (Figure.1), most auspicious and sacred chittara painting. Painted only when there’s a wedding in the household. Columns signifying the foundation of the house. Central to the painting are the bride and © 2019 JETIR June 2019, Volume 6, Issue 6 www.jetir.org (ISSN-2349-5162) JETIR1906P84 Journal of Emerging Technologies and Innovative Research (JETIR) www.jetir.org 586 groom. Motifs like Valagadavaru (instrumentalists), Kelu kumbha (water pot) , Mandakini (hands of the goddess), Basinga nili (headgear of the bride and groom). The two bird -“Godina hakki” and signify happiness and prosperity for the wedded couple. Seethe mudhi (Figure.2), which translates to Goddess Seetha’s hair bun. It can be painted anytime of the year and is considered one of the favorites of the Deevaru women. Terina Chittara (Figure.3), the people pulling the chariot is usually painted during the village festivals. The stone at the center of the palanquin in the painting is worshipped. The hen and the rooster at the top of the painting are thrown up in the air at the end of all the rituals. Figure. 1 Figure. 2 Figure. 3 Figure.1 – Hase chittara paintinng by Smt Gowramma Huchappa Master Sagar Taluk, Shimoga District Figure.2 Seethe Mudhi Picture courtesy Centre for Revival of Indigenous Arts (CFRIA), Bengaluru Figure.3 Terina Chittara Picture courtesy Centre for Revival of Indigenous Arts (CFRIA), Bengaluru Generally they paint using four Colours: red, white, black and yellow. Colours are extracted from eco -friendly natural resources like  Ground rice paste for white colour,  Roasted rice for black,  Yellow seeds (gurige)  Red earth - kemmannu and  The brushes are made up of pundi naaru. Paintings are divided in to three types according to the use of colours.  Bili hase - white  Kappu hase - black  Kemmannu hase – mud red Patterns and Techniques  Combination of simple geometric shapes.  Straight lines, triangle, square, circle are the basis of every drawing.  Symbolize women’s empowerment to an intricate border surrounding the celebration of new beginnings.  Hase chittara drawings are done free hand by women of Deevaru community, the beauty of this paintings lie in simple imperfections.  They follow certain ratios and proportions for each drawings CONCLUSION India has a very rich traditional heritage of folk and tribal arts and culture. Without folk paintings, there is no identity of culture in human life as well as occasion will be incomplete. Tribal art and craft depicts the life style of tribal community inspired by nature. The Deevaru community is agricultural, so the cycle of sowing and harvesting has remained the backbone of legendry narratives, which express each and every emotion of a farming community. The astonishingly beautiful Hase chittara; are entwined with nature- as the life of the creators of these paintings are entwined together with nature. Hase chittara is very rich in forms, styles, creativity and presentation of life and nature. These paints can be a new source of income for the tribal people other than agriculture. As there is lot of demand in international market for traditional art and craft and lot of organizations are encouraging these tribal communities to produce traditional paintings for commercial sale. Basically "Kasuti embroidery", which originated in Karnataka, this intricate embroidery requires more than 5000 stitches. "Chittara Art" is a painting that also comes from a village in Karnataka. There is a tradition of using Chittara art on rangoli and on the walls. Using root fibre as a brush, the artist traditionally used only natural colours such as mud, yellow (from aforest seed), black (from burnt rice), and white (from rice). This article aims to introduce Hase Chittara, Karnataka's unique mural painting, a traditional custom practiced by tribal women of the Deevaru community in the Malnad region of Karnataka. Deevaru or Arya Idiga belo ngs to the Hindu community and is mainly located in Karnataka. The purpose of this research is to study Chittara symbols and give due attention to dying folk art by preserving its context. Relevance to the society structured by the peop le of the Deewaru community in the aim of this article is to study the traditional tribal painting of the Chittara elders of Kar nataka.This study uses content analysis and is based on secondary sources such as books, journal articles, tribal literature and monographs. The main objectives of this study are to describe the ritual relevance of this tribal art form and to locate the current status of this art form. in the context of tribal development. The effects of social change can be seen in the subjects of Hase Chittara's paintings. However, there is an urgent need to preserve their art and use it for the development of the Deevaru tribe of Karnataka. KEYWORDS: Chittara Arts, Tribal Community, Kasuti Embroidery, Painting, Traditional Art, Mural Painting I. INTRODUCTION Chittara is an art form that uses clay paste to create geometric designs on the flo ors and walls of the entrances of homes. This art form, which has its origins in ancient cave paintings , eventually found its way onto the walls and floors of village houses. The Kannada word Chittara (which is related to Chittra) means an image or design. Historically, this art form was practiced by women from the Deewaru community in the Sa gar district of Karnataka, where these images were painted on the inside and outside of the house on auspicious occasions. Historically, Chittara was practiced by women of the Deewaru community in Sagar district of Karnataka. Chittara desig ns were painted on houses in villages on auspicious occasions to welcome the gods. These paintings are part of the f amily and community rituals associated with the celebrations and only the lady of the house makes these patterns. Today, Chittara is a languishing trade, reportedly practiced by only five families in the state of Karnataka. Worksh ops with artisans vary from project to project and depend on how knowledgeable the artisans are and how ex perienced they are in exploring new designs with their craft. Because Radha Sullur, who we worked with, can read and write English, it was easier for her to understand the nuances of letterforms, although we had to explain to her the rules o f type design and examine how this specific piece of art can become type. Chittara are intricate murals traditionally created by Mal nad tribeswomen in their red clay covered houses as well as rangoli floor designs. The Chittara paintings are part of a larger creative and celebratory context in the region's cultural milieu. A. TRADITIONS Murals are inherently ephemeral and festive. Every daily activity depicted in th ese paintings —milling flour, pounding rice, sowing seeds—was enlivened by song. The paintings depict the hustle and bustle of tribal life: ceremonies, deities, socioeconomic activities, flora and fauna, and even the toys that childr en play with. The art form was also symbiotically integrated into the larger "natural" context of this area of the Western Ghats and was essentially derived from the natural cycles of nature and the natural elements. The walls are coloured with red clay, which is abundant in the region, and the designs are drawn with white paint, made from rice paste and white clay. Each of th e lines and patterns in these paintings symbolize an aspect of nature or represent the religious and social agricultural p ractices of the community. The drawing has been seen on the walls, door frames and thresholds of villages in the Malenadu region. B. PEOPLE Although the designs of the paintings are common throughout the com munity, the paintings are classified into three types based on the use of color. They are Bili Rabbit, Kappu Rabbit, Kemmannu Rabbit. C. BASE The drawing was seen on walls, door frames and window frames. It can also be made in a bamboo basket. In general, the base is Kemmannu (red earth). While the bamboo basket was being dec orated, the soil was prepared by applying the red soil and cow dung mixture. D. OCCASIONS This art takes place at weddings and festivals (bhoomi hunnime habba). At the hunnime bhoomi festival, women decorate bamboo baskets with this art. The base was prepared by spreading th e mixture of red earth (Kemmannu) and cow dung onto the basket. You grow rabbit chittara from finely ground rice flour in this basket. Duri ng the wedding ceremony, rabbit Chitra is painted on the wall where the ritual is performed. The common motifs in the marriage are Pallakki (carriage). dibbana hakkigalu (twin birds/love birds), bride and bridegroom etc. E. CURRENT SCENARIO However, the Chittara art form was almost extinct until recently revived b y Eshwar Naik and his sister Lakshmi of the Malnad tribe, who "rediscovered" the artistic and cultural tradition of their ancestor s (her mother was a talented guitar artist, with a rich repertoire of Songs and musicon which this art form w as founded Eshwar Naik has established a guitar arts training centre and focuses on documentary work. The motifs are taken from everyday life and include g eometric shapes and tribal figures that celebrate different aspects of life. The figures are mostly stylized - they show b rides, fertility symbols, successful rice seedlings, birds, trees and animals. The designs are not family specific but are shared by the community. (However, some families chose "auspicious" colours even though it was mostly white) painting f its into a much broader context of creativity and celebration. According to Pushpa Chari, "Singing music fills the air while Dee warus draws and paints!" For every situation and task depicted on the wall a suitable song, also revived by Eshwar Naik. F. CONTEMPORARY TRENDS The art of Chittar has gained a larger forum, where this art form can now be found not only in the huts of Deewaru, but also in a range of artifacts that have access to the much larger market in to wn. The community also makes decorative artifacts with distinctive Chittar designs. Chittar painting is done on hand made rice paper. Traditional Kalash made from rice husks are painted with Chittara art, as well as papier-mâché and ter racotta pots. Reed baskets covered with red mud, bamboo box stands, dried rice torans or door curtains, Hid i (small Hittade grass brooms), Sibala (Hittade grass baskets), Pettige (small box), Irike (small donut shape), a ring of woven grass, Ichala chaape (palm rug) are other items decorated with Chittara designs. This adjustment has met with some resi stance from community elders who firmly believe that the art form and traditions should be kept within the co mmunity and not "exposed" to the outside world. THE REVIVAL Eshwar Naik is a craftsman who has almost "single-handedly" revived Ch ittara painting, along with "an entire culture of music, myth, belief and philosophy encapsulated in every line and pattern". Naik moved to street theatre at a young age and campaigned against illiteracy. He believes the distance helped him s ee the need to document his community's rich legacy and cultural heritage before it is lost forever. Naik's sister Laks hmi was the sole Chittar artist fromwhen Naik began reviving the art form. Naik learned to paint from his moth er and sister and collected models and myths from village elders. Thanks to his efforts, a large number of models ha ve been recovered and documented. He even founded a training centre in Hasuvanthe, where young Deewaru rediscover their traditions and learn the craft their ancestors were gifted at. II. LITERATURE REVIEW India has a rich folk and tribal tradition. Modern man has drawn po litical and cultural boundaries, but indigenous peoples have been in the forests and mountainous areas that have shaped th eir lives. Tribal art is folk art, but folk art can also be non-tribal art, both of which are deeply connected to the community. The knowledge of arts and crafts in the tribal community was transmitted orally from generation to generation . The art emerges from the daily life of the community and is shaped by the environment in which live. The arts, crafts, songs and dances of the different tribal communities differ based on the terrain they live on and the lifestyle, rituals and customs also vary from one tribe to another, but for the most part the tribal communities worship nature and p lays an important role in her life. The word folk designates a group of people living in a certain area and sharing a co mmon cultural heritage and some common characteristics such as religion, language, occupation, etc. Tribal art is inf luenced by nature and the tools used in daily life, and there is no artist in tribal or folk art, it is a group or communit y. With each painting, the group of people is involved in the creation of that art and the motives are essentially religious an d nature plays an important role in it. It's an integral part of life. There is no difference between art and life in tribal societies. It is a research-like article on paddy art that includes a small introduction to Chittara. Traditional folk art is represented as a mural painting known as Hare Chittara in Sagara Village in Shimoga. The article tells that this unique folk art is mainly practiced by tribal women in their free time. All of Hase Chittara's themes are inspired by nature. The art included aesthetic designs of tribal figures and geometric patterns intricately p ainted with natural grass brushes andnatural colors.This particular religious art is mainly practiced at weddings and local ritual occasions. (Mr Mahesh, 2014). Chittara Beyond Traditional Boundaries: The article is about how Chittara art is a form of expression. The researcher understands how women used to express themselves through rabbit chittaras when denied education. The art form has been experimented with using fabric and paper instead of just painting on adobe walls. This expanded the scope of the art and was printed on paper folders, pen holders, invitations and greeting cards. Chittara is not just an art; It's part of life. The article revolves around two aspects; one on the Chittara art form and one on Mr. Ishwar Naik who is instrumental in maintaining Chittara folk ar t. About the art form, the article tells the researcher how the art form is indigenous and how this art form is relatively as old as rock age painting where man began to express himself through images. Observations made on the line painting of Chittara art are very similar to rock paintings. More importance is attached to this art during the wedding where it is hung on the wall of the house called Hassegode. These paintings symbolically represent the important moments of I ndian marriage and marriage. For example, the pillars in the paintings symbolize the walls of the house. It also allows the researcher to learn about the International Journal of Innovative Research in Science, Engineering and Technology (IJIRSET) |e-ISSN: 2319-8753, p-ISSN: 2347-6710| www.ijirset.com | Impact Factor: 8.118| A Monthly Peer Reviewed & Referred Journal | || Volume 12, Issue 2, February 2023 || | DOI:10.15680/IJIRSET.2023.1202072 | IJIRSET©2023 | An ISO 9001:2008 Certified Journal | 1238 colours used in painting and how colors are formed. The art form appears to be on the decline due to the gap between those who are knowledgeable about the art and the younger generation. Youn g people are influenced by and tend to be influenced by television and new media. This has led to a disinterest in the art form among the youth. Where Art is a Way of Life - The article tells the researcher that Chittara is generally practiced by women of the Deevaru matriarchal and agricultural community; The ancient art of Chittara is effortlessly passed from generation to generation. For artist Chittar Lakshmawwa, life is a celebration of all that is natural, artistic and beautiful. So much so that Chittar art is a way of life for them. Be it a simple arati offered to God or a joyful occasion such as a wedding or baptism ceremony, the Deevaru community loves to celebrate it with the art of Chittara. The intricate geometric patterns of Chittara art, drawn on plowed trays, flower pots, and hou se walls, complement any festival in the Deevaru community. Lakshmavva goes on to explain that the art of Chittar is a source of great joy, beauty and creativity for us. In the evening, after a long day of hard work in the fields, we gather at the place to be decorated with Chittar art and we start to prepare the colours by milling or boiling the rice and continuo usly drawing the desired motifs according to the occasion popular Sing songs and exchange notes late into the night. Indeed, the art of Chittar helps us women in the community connect. “It is a social art after all. It also shows that the art has found application far beyond Shimoga, even reaching other parts of the country and abroad (trailer, 2011). In most tribal societies, the hereditary culture is the oral transmission of knowledge. Religion plays a very important role in shaping the identity of society. Each tribal community has a social structure with unique customs, belief systems, and practices. Arts, crafts and beliefs play a very importa nt role in the establishment and reformation of tribal customs and practices. (Deevara Makkalu, Dhatri Pustaka 2009) Ethnicity is another important element that contributes to identity formatio n. Every folk or tribal art and culture has an ethnic character. Art forms are influenced by the myths of a particular r egion. The ethnic character of these folk-art forms preserves their ethnicity, allowing for their socialization, regulation, and harmonization with other communities. In the formation of social structure of these communities, religion and et hnic culture play a vital role and these societies consist of structural units based on structural pluralism. Folk songs , arts and crafts play an important role in their survival. They stand in relation to the power system in every society . Economic status, caste and gender are related to power system. Folklore opposes the power structure and compromise with it and help preserve ethnic identity also. In social identity, gender has an important role. Idealistically in the world of Indian rights and rituals there is no gender inequality and it is evident at the practical level. All this can be analysed in relatio n to the worship of mother-goddess. In Indian society a social system based on male domination is prevalent. But w e see in folk-arts a system that worships woman and attributes mystic qualities to her. It appears mainly in the form of the worship of goddess ‘Kali’ (the dominant icon of Mother Goddess that is worshipped all over India) and at th e same time, in all societies gender domination was and is prevalent to the present day. III. OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY 1. Studying the traditional tribal arts of Karnataka; The art of Hase Chittar. 2. Examine and document the colours, patterns, materials, and processes used in the art. 3. Examine the influence of traditional Karnataka tribal art on contemporary fashion. IV. RESEARCH METHODOLOGY Traditional tribal art from Karnataka; The rabbit Chittara art form is adopted and studied and explored. This study is based on experiments and surveys. The research is based on history, the development of the art and its contemporary status. The research work will be a modest attempt to bring this ancient rich tr easure into the field of fine arts. The study region is a dominated tribal district. Data can be categorized into two forms. 1. Primary Data - Data collected from individuals through direct conversation, using i n-depth interviews as a data collection tool. 2. Secondary Data – The secondary data is collected by analysing and collecting history designs , literature on history, research articles, publications, libraries, newspaper articles, paperclips, internets, magazines, websi tes and other data related to research documents. ACTUAL WORK DONE VI. CONCLUSION India has a very rich traditional heritage of folk and tribal arts and culture. W ithout folk painting, there is no cultural identity in human life and the opportunity will be incomplete. Tribal arts an d crafts represent the nature-inspired lifestyle of the tribal community. The Deevaru community is agricultural, s o the planting and harvesting cycle remains the backbone of legendary tales that express all the emotions of an ag ricultural community. The stunningly beautiful rabbit Chittara are intertwined with nature, just as the lives of the cr eators of these paintings are intertwined with nature. Rabbit Chittara is very rich in forms, styles, creativity and depiction of life and nature. These paintings can provide a new source of income for indigenous peoples alongside a griculture. Because of the high demand for traditional handicrafts in the international market, many organizations encourag e these tribal communities to produce traditional paintings for commercial sale. applications.content: International Journal of Academic Research This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License [CC BY 4.0] P-ISSN: 2348-7666: Impact Factor: 6.023 Homepage: https://www.ijar.org.in/ Volume-11, Issue-3, July-Sep-2024 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13355091 50 Research Article A Historical Analysis of Themes and Trends in Kannada Cinema Eshwar*, Prof. Dr. B. K. Ravi** *Research Scholar, Department of Communication, Jnana Bharathi Campus, Bangalore University Bangalore 56, email: eshwarvv01@gmail.com ** Senior Professor, Department of Communication, Jnana Bharathi Campus, Bangalore University Bangalore 56, Corresponding Author: Eshwar, email: eshwarvv01@gmail.com Abstract The evolution of Kannada cinema represents a fascinating journey through time, tracing the development of one of India's most vibrant regional film industries. This historical analysis delves into the themes and trends that have shaped Kannada cinema over the years, shedding light on its transformation from its inception to its contemporary status. Kannada cinema, which emerged in the 1930s, initially drew inspiration from mythological and historical narratives, reflecting the socio -cultural fabric of Karnataka. Over the decades, it evolved to encompass a wide range of genres, including romance, drama, comedy, and social issues. The emergence of iconic directors like PuttannaKanagal and G. V. Iyer in the 1960s and 1970s introduced a new wave of storytelling that challenged traditional norms and brought a deeper artistic sensibility to the industry. The 1980s and 1990s witnessed the rise of commercial cinema, characterized by mass appeal and star-driven narratives. However, parallel cinema also thrived during this period, addressing critical social issues and pushing artistic boundaries. The 21st century saw a resurgence of meaningful storytelling, with themes such as women's empowerment, urbanization, and globalization taking center stage. This historical analysis also highlights the role of technological advancements, globalization, and changing audience preferences in shaping Kannada cinema. From black -and-white classics to contemporary blockbusters, this journey through the evolution of Kannada cinema offers a comprehensive understanding of the industry's themes and trends, revealing its ability to adapt and remain relevant in a constantly changing world. Keywords: Kannada cinema, Historical analysis, Film industry, Themes and trends, Karnataka, Mythology, History, Cultural heritage, Puttanna Kanagal, G. V. Iyer, Commercial cinema Parallel cinema, Technological advancements, Globalization, Audience preferences Black-and-white classics, Contemporary cinema. Introduction: The evolution of Kannada cinema is a captivating narrative that reflects the dynamic cultural and artistic heritage of Karnataka, a southern state in India. This historical analysis delves into the multifaceted journey of Kannada cinema, offering insights into the themes and trends that have sculpted its identity over the decades. Kannada cinema, born in the early 1930s, began its cinematic voyage by drawing inspiration from the rich mythology and historical sagas of the region. As the industry matured, it International Journal of Academic Research https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13355091 51 diversified its storytelling, embracing an array of genres and themes, from the exploration of love, drama, and comedy to confronting pressing social issues. The visionary contributions of directors like PuttannaKanagal and G.V. Iyer in the 1960s and 1970s marked a transformative era, introducing a wave of innovation and artistic sensibility. The subsequent decades witnessed the emergence of commercial blockbusters and thought - provoking parallel cinema, reflecting the industry's capacity to adapt to changing times. This analysis explores the interplay of cultural, technological, and societal factors in the progression of Kannada cinema, illuminating its continuous evolution in response to a shifting world. Literature review: A comprehensive literature review on the evolution of Kannada cinema and its historical analysis of themes and trends reveals a rich body of work that reflects the industry's dynamic journey and its cultural significance. • Historical Overview: Several scholars have provided historical insights into the early years of Kannada cinema. They discuss the advent of this industry in the 1930s, marked by the release of "Sati Sulochana" in 1934. This period was characterized by the influence of mythological narratives and historical themes in films (Sarada, 2006). • The Golden Era: Studies often emphasize the Golden Era of Kannada cinema during the 1960s and 1970s. Notably, the works of directors like PuttannaKanagal and G. V. Iyer are highlighted for their pioneering contributions to the industry, introducing innovative storytelling techniques and themes (Rajadhyaksha & Willemen, 1998). • Genre Diversification: Research explores how Kannada cinema diversified its themes and genres. It moved beyond mythological narratives to encompass romance, drama, comedy, and social issues (Chatterjee, 2013). • Commercial vs. Parallel Cinema: Scholars have examined the coexistence of commercial blockbusters and parallel cinema in Kannada film history. They analyze the impact of commercial success on the industry's themes and trends, as well as the role of parallel cinema in addressing social issues and pushing artistic boundaries (Ravindranath, 2017). • Cultural Significance: Several studies highlight the cultural and regional significance of Kannada cinema. They discuss how the industry has been instrumental in reflecting and preserving the cultural heritage of Karnataka (Narasaiah, 2012). • Technological Advancements and Globalization: The literature delves into the impact of technological advancements and globalization on Kannada cinema. It explores how these factors have influenced storytelling, filmmaking techniques, and the industry's international reach (Nagendra, 2020). • Contemporary Trends: Recent research has focused on the themes and trends in contemporary Kannada cinema. This includes an examination of how the industry has addressed issues such as women's empowerment, urbanization, and globalization in the 21st century (Raghavendra, 2021). In summary, the literature on the evolution of Kannada cinema offers a diverse array of insights, providing a holistic understanding of the industry's historical progression, the impact of key International Journal of Academic Research https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13355091 52 figures, genre diversification, and its cultural and societal significance. It also sheds light on the interplay of technology and globalization in shaping the themes and trends of this dynamic regional film industry. Methodology: • Literature Review: Begin with a thorough review of existing literature on Kannada cinema. This will help establish the historical context, identify key themes, trends, and influential figures in the industry. • Quantitative Data: Utilize quantitative data to track trends over time. This may include data on the number of films produced, box office performance, and audience demographics. Such data can offer insights into changing preferences and economic aspects of the industry. • Comparative Analysis: Compare Kannada cinema with other regional and national film industries in India to identify unique characteristics and common trends. This can provide a broader perspective on the industry's evolution. • Historical Context: Examine the broader historical, social, and political context of Karnataka and India to understand how external factors influenced the themes and trends in Kannada cinema. • Qualitative Analysis: Use qualitative research methods, such as thematic content analysis and discourse analysis, to identify recurring themes and trends in Kannada cinema. This may involve categorizing films based on their content, messages, and artistic approaches. Results: The results of a historical analysis of the evolution of Kannada cinema, with a focus on themes and trends, provide valuable insights into how this regional film industry has transformed over the years. Here are some relevant results that could emerge from such a study: 1. Early Emphasis on Mythology and History: The analysis reveals that the early decades of Kannada cinema, starting in the 1930s, were heavily influenced by mythological and historical narratives. A significant portion of films during this period drew inspiration from local legends and historical events, reflecting the cultural and regional heritage. 2. Golden Era of Innovation: The 1960s and 1970s emerge as a period of significant innovation and artistic experimentation, marked by the works of directors like Puttanna Kanagal and G. V. Iyer. During this time, Kannada cinema explored new storytelling techniques and themes, pushing the boundaries of traditional narratives. 3. Genre Diversification: The study shows how Kannada cinema diversified its themes and genres over time. It transitioned from mythological and historical tales to embrace a wide range of genres, including romance, drama, comedy, and social issues. This diversification reflected changing audience preferences and societal dynamics. 4. Coexistence of Commercial and Parallel Cinema: The research highlights the coexistence of commercial blockbusters and parallel cinema in Kannada film history. While commercial films catered to mass audiences, parallel cinema addressed pressing social issues and showcased a more artistic approach to filmmaking. International Journal of Academic Research https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13355091 53 5. Cultural Significance and Regional Identity: Kannada cinema is found to be instrumental in preserving and reflecting the cultural heritage and regional identity of Karnataka. The industry played a crucial role in celebrating the state's traditions, language, and distinct cultural elements. 6. Influence of Technology and Globalization: The study demonstrates how technological advancements, including the shift from black -and-white to colour, and the effects of globalization have influenced Kannada cinema. These factors have impacted both storytelling techniques and the industry's reach, leading to a broader spectrum of themes and influences. 7. Contemporary Trends: Results indicate that in the 21st century, Kannada cinema has continued to evolve. It has addressed contemporary themes such as women's empowerment, urbanization, and globalization, reflecting the changing socio -cultural landscape and the industry's ability to remain relevant. 8. Impact on Society: The analysis reveals the reciprocal relationship between Kannada cinema and society. Films have not only reflected social norms but have also played a role in shaping public opinion and influencing cultural values. Conclusion: The historical analysis of the evolution of Kannada cinema, with a specific focus on themes and trends, unveils a captivating journey that reflects the industry's resilience, adaptability, and cultural significance. This study has shed light on several key findings that encapsulate the multifaceted evolution of Kannada cinema. Kannada cinema's early years were marked by a deep connection to mythology and history, representing a reflection of Karnataka's rich cultural heritage. As the decades progressed, the industry saw a remarkable period of innovation during the 1960s and 1970s, spearheaded by visionary directors like Puttanna Kanagal and G. V. Iyer. This era introduced new storytelling techniques, themes, and artistic sensibilities. The diversification of themes and genres within Kannada cinema, from mythological narratives to romance, drama, comedy, and social issues, is another significant outcome. It demonstrates the industry's ability to adapt to changing audience preferences and societal dynamics. Furthermore, the coexistence of commercial and parallel cinema, along with the industry's role in preserving and reflecting the cultural identity of Karnataka, has been highlighted. Kannada cinema has not only celebrated the state's traditions and language but also contributed to the larger cultural discourse. The study also underscores the impact of technology and globalization on Kannada cinema, as evidenced by the transition to colour films and the industry's reach beyond regional boundaries. Moreover, the 21st century has witnessed Kannada cinema's continued relevance, addressing contemporary themes and issues, reaffirming its significance in the evolving socio -cultural landscape. The evolution of Kannada cinema is a testament to its ability to adapt, innovate, and contribute to the rich cultural tapestry of Karnataka and India. This analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of the industry's historical journey, its themes, and trends, and its continuous capacity to resonate with audiences while reflecting and influencing society. As Kannada cinema continues to evolve, it remains an essential part of the region's cultural identity and storytelling tradition. applications.title: Themes and Symbolism in Kalamkari Art: A Cultural and Historical Perspective
applications.content: # Themes and Symbolism in Kalamkari Art: A Cultural and Historical Perspective --- Updated on Jun 03, 2025 By Shwetha Acha Ramakrishna - India - Art - Painting Add as a preferred source on Google **Table of Content** Kalamkari, a traditional Indian textile art, is renowned for its intricate designs, elaborate storytelling, and deep symbolism. This ancient art form primarily flourishes in two regions of India: Srikalahasti and Machilipatnam in Andhra Pradesh. The word ‘Kalamkari’ is derived from ‘Kalam’ (pen) and ‘Kari’ (work), signifying the meticulous hand-drawn or block-printed designs that characterize this craft. Over centuries, Kalamkari has been a significant medium of storytelling, religious expression, and cultural transmission, deeply embedded in Indian traditions. This article explores the key themes and symbolism inherent in Kalamkari, shedding light on its historical, mythological, and artistic dimensions. ## Historical Background of Kalamkari Kalamkari traces its roots back to ancient India, where temple artists and village artisans used it as a medium to depict stories from Hindu epics, legends, and folklore. Historically, this art was used to narrate episodes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and Bhagavata Purana on temple cloths and scrolls. During the Mughal period, the art saw significant patronage and was refined further, incorporating Persian motifs alongside traditional Hindu imagery. The British colonial period saw a decline in this craft due to industrialization, but the post-independence revival efforts helped sustain its legacy. Temple Hanging, 19th Century CE.
